opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I was at MIT, I was quite optimistic about a "physics of AI," though I saw it as a long-term project rather than something that would pay off overnight.

My background is in physics, and what attracted me to the idea is that physicists are very good at one thing: facing a complicated system they don't fully understand, they find the right simplifications, run controlled experiments, and extract regularities, sometimes even laws. Neural networks looked to me like exactly that kind of system. We build them, but we don't really understand why they work. So it felt natural to treat them the way we treat nature: observe, find phenomena, build toy models, and try to explain them.

At the time, I thought there were two main approaches in the field. One was the engineering approach: scale things up and see what happens. That's been enormously successful. The other was the mathematical approach: prove theorems about learning. That's rigorous, but it often lags far behind practice, because the assumptions you need for a proof don't match real systems. I felt there was a gap in between, and physics fits there. Physics isn't as rigorous as math, but it's much more connected to phenomena. You don't need a full proof to make progress. You need good intuition, good experiments, and models that are "right enough" to predict something.

So my view was that a physics of AI would focus on phenomena first. Things like grokking, scaling laws, how representations form, why some structures emerge during training. If you study these carefully in simple settings, you can often find surprisingly clean explanations. Some of my work on grokking, for example, came from asking: what is the network actually learning internally, and can we see the structure of the representation? Once you look at it the right way, things that seemed mysterious become much more understandable.

I'll also be honest that there were challenges. One was a cultural question: the AI community moves very fast and values benchmarks and performance, while physics-style understanding is slower and its value isn't always immediately visible. Another was that AI systems aren't like nature in one important sense. Nature's laws are fixed, but in AI we keep changing the architectures and the data. So there's always a risk that what you discover is specific to a particular setup and doesn't generalize.

Still, I believed, and I still believe, that understanding matters. If we want AI that is more efficient, more interpretable, and safer, we can't rely on trial and error forever. At some point we need something like a science of these systems. Physics has a long tradition of turning messy observations into understanding, so I saw real promise in bringing that mindset to AI.

r001.rationale: The response says Liu was optimistic about a physics of AI, but does not say a small group of academics could formulate it.

r002.rationale: He says that to achieve more efficient, interpretable, and safer AI, “we can't rely on trial and error forever” and need a science of these systems, linking physics-style understanding to reducing that reliance.

fable-5.1.text:
When I was at MIT, I was honestly quite optimistic, but it was an optimism mixed with a lot of uncertainty about what "physics of AI" actually meant.

My background is in physics, and I was working with Max Tegmark, so naturally we kept asking: can we treat neural networks the way physicists treat a physical system? Not as a black box you poke at, but as something with laws, with structure you can write down. Things like scaling laws, phase transitions during training, grokking, the way symmetries show up in learned representations: these all looked like physics phenomena to us. Physicists have a reflex of looking for a few simple variables that govern a complicated system, and I believed, and still believe, that deep learning has that kind of hidden simplicity.

At the same time, I was aware of the counterargument. Physics works because nature doesn't change its mind. Neural networks are engineered artifacts, and the architectures and training recipes change every year. So there was always this worry that whatever "law" you discover is really a law about one particular architecture at one particular moment, and it evaporates when the field moves on.

What convinced me the project was worthwhile was the interpretability angle. Work like the Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks project, and the earlier work on AI Feynman, came from the idea that if we can make models more transparent, more like equations a scientist could read, then the physics of AI stops being just a description and becomes a design principle. You don't only observe the system, you build it to be understandable.

So my view at MIT was something like: the field was pre-Newtonian. Lots of beautiful empirical regularities, very little unifying theory yet. That's a frustrating place to be, but historically it's also the most exciting place to be, because it means the big ideas haven't been found.

r001.rationale: The response describes Liu and Tegmark exploring whether neural networks have simple governing variables, but does not state that Liu believed a small group of academics could formulate a physics of AI.

r002.rationale: The response says interpretability could make physics of AI a design principle, but does not say it would reduce reliance on trial and error in designing or training models.

astra-6.text:
When I was at MIT, I was optimistic about the possibility, but I thought the question was how to make it concrete. In physics, we often start with a complicated system and look for a simple model that captures something essential. I felt we could take a similar approach to AI: study a controlled setting, identify a phenomenon, and try to explain why it happens.

That doesn’t necessarily mean we’ll find one elegant theory that explains all of deep learning. But we might find useful principles piece by piece. For me, that was the exciting prospect—understanding what these systems learn and how that understanding might help us build better ones.

r001.rationale: The response says Liu was optimistic about a physics of AI, but does not state that a small group of academics could formulate it.

r002.rationale: The response says understanding AI might help build better systems, but does not say this would reduce reliance on trial and error.

sol-6.1.text:
When I was at MIT, I was optimistic about the idea, but I didn’t have a clear picture of what a physics of AI would look like. In physics, you try to find simple principles beneath complicated behavior. I wondered whether we could do something similar for neural networks: identify a few concepts that explain how they learn and why certain behaviors emerge.

The challenge was finding the right questions. A neural network is a system we construct, and we can change its architecture, its data, or its training procedure. So what should count as a general law? For me, the prospect was exciting precisely because that was still open. You could study a small, controlled example and hope to discover something that carried over to much larger systems.

r001.rationale: The response says the idea was exciting and discusses studying controlled examples, but it does not say that a small group of academics could formulate a physics of AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses finding general principles, but does not say that a physics of AI would reduce reliance on trial and error in model design or training.
